body.heading: Momentum likes evidence
paragraphs: On days when everything feels large and tangled, motivation is hard to summon by argument. But it responds well to evidence. One small thing, completely finished, is evidence: I start things and I finish them.
That is why a tiny completed task early in the day can loosen a whole morning. It is not magic; it is your brain updating its expectations based on the most recent data point.

body.heading: Choose the right small thing
paragraphs: The best opener is small, visible and genuinely finished in under ten minutes: reply to the one-line email, water the plants, file the pile, make the appointment. Avoid “small” tasks that secretly contain decisions, like tidying a drawer — those are projects in disguise.
It also helps if the small thing is real, not staged. Crossing off something trivial you added just to cross it off fools nobody, least of all you.

body.heading: Then ride the slope, gently
paragraphs: Straight after the small finish, move to the day’s main task while the momentum is warm — ideally with a sprint timer and your later list beside you. The opener works because it points somewhere.
Not every day needs this trick, and it is not a cure for genuinely overloaded days. But as a way of unfreezing a stuck start, one honest small finish is hard to beat.

takeaway: When the day feels stuck, finish one small real thing — then start the big one while the proof is fresh.
